# Wisdom of Solomon — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Anonymous Alexandrian Jewish philosopher (writing as Solomon) |
| **Date** | c. 100 BCE – 50 CE (most likely c. 50 BCE – 30 CE) |
| **Audience** | Educated Diaspora Jews in Alexandria, Egypt |
| **Genre** | Philosophical wisdom poetry / theological treatise |
| **Timeline** | Composed in Greek in Alexandria; fictional setting is Solomonic Israel |
| **In One Sentence** | An anonymous Jewish philosopher, writing in the voice of Solomon, argues with breathtaking intellectual ambition that Wisdom herself is the divine force who governs history, guarantees immortality to the righteous, and exposes the folly of both apostasy and idolatry. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

Alexandria in the first century BCE was perhaps the most intellectually alive city in the world. It was home to the Great Library, to the famous Museum where scholars worked in royal patronage, and to one of the largest Jewish communities in the ancient world — a community that had been speaking Greek for two or three generations, that read Torah in Greek (the Septuagint had been produced largely for their use), and that was in constant, electrifying, sometimes destabilizing dialogue with Hellenistic philosophy. Stoicism, Platonism, and Epicureanism were not distant abstractions for the Jewish scholars of Alexandria — they were the intellectual water everyone swam in. The question was not whether to engage Greek philosophy, but how.

The Wisdom of Solomon is the most ambitious answer to that question that Jewish antiquity produced. Its anonymous author was almost certainly a highly educated Alexandrian Jew who had absorbed not only the Hebrew scriptures but also the philosophical vocabulary of Middle Platonism — the tradition that stood between the original Plato and the later Neo-Platonists. The book's concepts of the soul's immortality, the body as a "tent" temporarily housing the soul (9:15), the divine spirit permeating all things, and Wisdom as a cosmic mediating principle all reflect engagement with Platonic ideas. But the author is not simply Platonizing Judaism; the effort is in the other direction — using the tools of Greek philosophy to articulate and defend a distinctively Jewish theological vision.

The immediate pressure behind the book is the experience of a minority community under cultural and sometimes physical threat. Jews in Alexandria faced periodic persecution, social pressure to abandon Jewish practice, the seductive pull of Hellenistic culture, and — perhaps most existentially troubling — the apparent prosperity of those who had abandoned Torah. Why do the righteous suffer? Why do the wicked flourish? These are the questions that drive the opening chapters, and the author's answer is not a retreat into simple piety but a philosophically sophisticated argument: the immortality of the soul means that what looks like the final verdict — the death of the righteous person — is not final at all. The wicked have already received everything they will ever get. The righteous are only beginning.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The book opens (chapters 1–5) with what scholars call the "Book of Eschatology" — an urgent argument against apostasy. Real people were leaving Jewish practice, and the author writes to them directly, or writes to those tempted by their example. The apostate's reasoning, presented with uncomfortable sympathy in chapter 2, is essentially Epicurean: life is short, death is final, there is no accountability, so eat and drink and seize pleasure while you can. "Our name will be forgotten in time," they say, "and no one will remember our works" (2:4). The author does not dismiss this as crude hedonism — he presents it as a sophisticated position that follows logically from a denial of immortality. His counter-argument is equally philosophical: if the soul is immortal, then everything the apostate calculates as gain is actually loss, and the suffering of the righteous person is not tragedy but the price of a reward that vastly exceeds it.

The middle section (chapters 6–9) pivots to a meditation on Wisdom herself — the great "Praise of Wisdom" that constitutes one of the most remarkable theological poems in all of Jewish literature. Here the author elaborates Wisdom (Greek: Sophia) as a personal divine figure who "pervades and penetrates all things" (7:24), who "reaches mightily from one end of the earth to the other, and she orders all things well" (8:1). She is the "reflection of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness" (7:26). She was present at creation, beside the divine throne, and she comes to those who seek her — specifically to kings, urging them to seek her rather than power alone. The persona of Solomon is deployed here to make the point: the wisest and most powerful king knew that Wisdom was worth more than all his wealth.

The final section (chapters 10–19) retells the Exodus as a demonstration of Wisdom at work in history, showing how she guided the patriarchs and delivered Israel from Egypt while judging their oppressors. This is midrash of a high order — a creative rereading of the scriptural story through a philosophical lens. The plagues of Egypt are re-examined in detail (chs. 16–19) to show a precise theological logic: the same element that punished Egypt blessed Israel. Water drowned the Egyptians; the same water gave Israel to drink. The book closes on this note of divine irony: creation itself is aligned with the purposes of the God who made it.

---

## How to Read This Book

The Wisdom of Solomon is not a narrative — it is an extended poem and argument, and it rewards slow, ruminative reading rather than the kind of reading one gives to a story. The book has three distinct movements, and each requires a different orientation from the reader.

The first movement (chapters 1–5) is urgent and confrontational. The author is writing against a position — the position of those who have concluded that life is meaningless and accountability is an illusion — and he writes with the energy of a debater who has thought through his opponent's arguments carefully. The famous speech of the wicked in chapter 2 ("our time is a passing shadow," 2:5) is worth reading as a standalone poem, because the author wants the reader to feel its force before dismantling it. Chapters 3–5 contain some of the most moving passages in all of deuterocanonical literature, including the celebrated opening of chapter 3: "But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died, and their departure was thought to be a disaster, and their going from us to be their destruction; but they are at peace."

The second movement (chapters 6–9) is lyrical and rapturous. The Praise of Wisdom in chapter 7 is one of those passages that justifies the entire book — a sustained meditation on divine Wisdom that twenty-two attributes are barely enough to describe. Read it aloud if possible; this is poetry designed to be heard. Chapter 9, the prayer of Solomon for Wisdom, is one of the finest prayers in Jewish literature, and was read as such across many centuries.

The third movement (chapters 10–19) is typological and midrashic. The reader benefits from knowing the Exodus story well, because the author is not retelling it but reinterpreting it — pointing out patterns and meanings that a surface reading misses. The shift in style (more prose-like, more expository) may feel like a drop in intensity after the soaring poetry of chapters 7–9, but the theological payoff — the demonstration that Wisdom is not an abstract principle but a real force at work in the history of a real people — is essential to the book's argument.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

**Proverbs 8 (Wisdom as divine personification):** The foundation for the Wisdom of Solomon's portrait of Sophia is Proverbs 8, where Wisdom speaks in the first person as a figure present at creation: "When he marked out the foundations of the earth, then I was beside him, like a master workman" (Prov 8:29–30). The author of Wisdom takes this portrait and enormously elaborates it, giving Wisdom attributes drawn partly from Hellenistic philosophical language but rooted in this older Israelite tradition. Reading Proverbs 8 alongside Wisdom 7–8 illuminates both.

**Job 28 (Where shall Wisdom be found?):** The great "Hymn to Wisdom" in Job 28 asks where Wisdom can be found in a world that seems random and unjust — a question that stands directly behind the Wisdom of Solomon's entire argument. The author's answer is more developed and philosophically specific than Job's, but the question is the same.

**John 1 (Logos theology):** The most important New Testament connection. The Gospel of John's Prologue — "In the beginning was the Word (Logos), and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... all things were made through him" (John 1:1–3) — draws directly on the Jewish Wisdom tradition that the Wisdom of Solomon represents. John transposes the feminine Sophia into the masculine Logos, but the theological architecture is identical: a divine figure present at creation, through whom all things were made, who "came to his own" in history. Many scholars argue that John's Prologue is the single most direct New Testament engagement with Wisdom of Solomon's theology.

**Romans 1 (Idolatry polemic):** Paul's extended argument in Romans 1:18–32 — that the Gentiles suppressed their knowledge of God, exchanged natural worship for idolatry, and were given over to moral disorder as a consequence — follows the logic and even some of the specific language of Wisdom 13–14's polemic against idol worship. The sequence (knowledge of God available through creation → rejection of that knowledge → moral degradation as consequence) is essentially the same in both texts.

**Hebrews 1 (Image of God's glory):** Hebrews 1:3 describes the Son as "the radiance of God's glory and the exact imprint of his nature" — language strikingly close to Wisdom 7:26's "reflection of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness." The Wisdom tradition is one of the primary conceptual reservoirs from which the New Testament authors drew their Christology.

**Isaiah 40–55 (Servant and suffering righteous):** The portrait of the suffering righteous person in Wisdom 2–5 — innocent, mocked, condemned, apparently defeated, but ultimately vindicated — echoes the Servant Songs of Isaiah with remarkable precision. "Let us see if his words are true... for if the righteous man is God's child, he will help him" (Wis 2:17–18) picks up language from Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22. Early Christian readers naturally read both texts as pointing to Jesus.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The pseudonymous authorship — writing as Solomon — is not deception in any modern sense. In the Jewish wisdom tradition, attributing a text to Solomon was a literary convention that situated the work in the lineage of Solomonic wisdom literature (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs). Ancient readers were not confused about this; they understood it as genre signaling. The convention allowed the author to speak with the full authority of the wisdom tradition while pursuing thoroughly contemporary concerns. Modern readers who find this troubling are applying a standard of authorial transparency that simply did not exist in antiquity.

The book's gender of Wisdom — consistently feminine in Greek (Sophia) and in the underlying Hebrew tradition (Chokmah) — is not incidental. The author has chosen a feminine divine figure as his primary theological concept, and the meditation on Wisdom in chapters 7–9 is written with unmistakable erotic tenderness: Solomon "loved her and sought her from my youth; I desired to take her for my bride" (8:2). This is not metaphor for abstract intellectual pursuits — it is a deliberate use of the language of desire and marriage to describe the human relationship with divine Wisdom. The same tradition underlies the Song of Songs. The masculine ego of the text (Solomon speaking) is in a relationship of longing and pursuit toward a feminine divine figure. Flattening this into mere allegory loses something essential.

The book's engagement with Greek philosophy is sophisticated enough to fool careful modern readers into thinking it has been co-opted by Hellenism. It has not. The author uses Platonic and Stoic concepts (the immortal soul, the world-soul, the four cardinal virtues named in 8:7) but consistently bends them to serve Jewish theological ends. The God of this book is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — the one who acts in history, who chose Israel, who defeated Pharaoh. The Greek philosophical concepts are tools, not conclusions.

The polemic against idolatry in chapters 13–15 is one of the most sophisticated analyses of the psychology of idolatry in all of ancient literature. The author distinguishes three types: nature worship (admiring creation without seeing the Creator — the most forgivable), craftsman's pride (the carpenter who uses half a tree for fuel and half to make an idol — Wisdom 13:11–14, anticipating Isaiah 44's identical satire), and fully developed cult idolatry (the most spiritually deadly). This taxonomy is not mere polemics; it is a serious attempt to understand how intelligent people come to worship what they have made, and the analysis has lost none of its relevance.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

The Wisdom of Solomon was written in Greek — there is no known Hebrew or Aramaic original, and no serious scholar believes one existed. This alone placed it outside the emerging Hebrew-language canon of the Tanakh. By the time Jewish scholars at Jamnia (c. 90 CE) were consolidating the Hebrew Bible canon, books without Hebrew originals were already being set aside, and the Wisdom of Solomon — however widely read and admired — did not pass the test.

In Christian history the book's influence was enormous, and it was treated as Scripture by many early Church Fathers. Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and Augustine all quoted it with scriptural authority. It was included in Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus — two of the oldest surviving Greek manuscripts of the Bible. The Latin Vulgate included it, and the Council of Trent (1546) formally defined it as canonical for Roman Catholics under the name "Book of Wisdom."

Protestant reformers followed the Hebrew canon principle: if it was not in the Hebrew Tanakh, it was not Scripture, regardless of how widely it had been used in the Church. Luther placed it in his "Apocrypha" section — books worth reading but not equal to Scripture. The Church of England's Thirty-Nine Articles (1562) adopted a similar position. Most Protestant Bibles today either omit it entirely or place it in an Apocrypha section.

Eastern Orthodox Christianity treats Wisdom of Solomon as fully deuterocanonical — part of the Old Testament — and it is read in the liturgy. Its influence on Orthodox theology, particularly in the developed traditions of divine Wisdom (Sophia theology), has been profound and ongoing.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| c. 950 BCE | Traditional date of Solomon's reign — the fictional persona of the book's author |
| c. 250–200 BCE | Septuagint translation of Torah completed in Alexandria for the Jewish Diaspora |
| c. 167–164 BCE | Maccabean revolt — the broader context of Jewish resistance to Hellenization |
| c. 100–50 BCE | Probable composition of Wisdom of Solomon in Alexandria |
| c. 50 BCE – 30 CE | Alternative (and widely held) dating window for the book's composition |
| c. 30–60 CE | New Testament authors draw on Wisdom tradition (Paul in Romans 1, John's Prologue, Hebrews 1) |
| c. 90 CE | Jewish canon discussions at Jamnia; books without Hebrew originals effectively excluded |
| c. 200–400 CE | Early Church Fathers (Clement, Origen, Augustine) quote Wisdom as authoritative Scripture |
| c. 382–405 CE | Jerome's Vulgate includes Wisdom of Solomon; Jerome notes its disputed status |
| 1546 CE | Council of Trent formally declares Wisdom of Solomon deuterocanonical for Roman Catholics |
| 1611 CE | King James Bible includes Wisdom of Solomon in the Apocrypha section |
